Midge Survival for Motorcycle Tourers

The Highland midge (Culicoides impunctatus) is Scotland's most fearsome resident. These tiny biting insects swarm in their billions from late May to September, and they've driven more tourers to despair than rain and mechanical failure combined. But with the right knowledge and preparation, you can coexist with them.

When Are They Active?

  • Season: Late May to September. Peak: June to August.
  • Time of day: Dawn and dusk are worst. They're less active in midday heat and bright sunshine.
  • Conditions: Still, humid, overcast days bring the worst swarms. Wind disperses them — a breeze of 5mph or more keeps them grounded.

Where Are They Worst?

  • West Highlands (Torridon, Kintail, Knoydart) — the dampest areas with the most midges
  • Anywhere near standing water, bogs, or damp woodland
  • Sheltered valleys and glens with no wind
  • The east coast and mountain summits are generally less affected

Repellent That Actually Works

  • Smidge: The UK-developed repellent specifically targeting Scottish midges. Contains Saltidin (Icaridin). Highly effective.
  • Avon Skin So Soft (Dry Oil Spray): An accidental midge repellent discovered by Royal Marines. Moisturiser that midges hate. Widely used and genuinely effective.
  • DEET-based repellents: Strong and effective but can damage plastics and synthetics. Use carefully near motorcycle gear.
  • Citronella: Mild repellent. Better than nothing but not as effective as Smidge or DEET.

Physical Defences

  • Midge head net: A fine mesh net worn over your head. Looks ridiculous but works perfectly. Weighs nothing. Essential for camp setup.
  • Long sleeves and trousers: Cover all exposed skin at camp. Midges can't bite through clothing.
  • Midge-proof tent: Ensure your tent's mesh is fine enough to exclude midges (standard mosquito mesh is too coarse). Inner-first tent designs let you dive in and zip up quickly.

Touring Tactics

  • Camp on high ground or exposed sites where breeze keeps midges away
  • Choose coastal camping over inland — sea breezes disperse midges
  • Avoid stopping near standing water at dawn and dusk
  • Keep your helmet visor down when stopped in midge areas
  • Set up camp quickly and get inside the tent before dusk
  • Cook and eat inside a well-ventilated tent porch if midges are bad
Check the Scottish Midge Forecast (smidgeup.com) before your tour. It provides a 5-day midge activity forecast by region. It's the most useful weather forecast in Scotland for outdoor enthusiasts.

Midge-Free Activities

When midges are intolerable, switch to activities they can't spoil. Riding itself is midge-free — at any speed above walking pace, midges can't keep up. It's only when you stop that they descend. Plan your stops at breezy viewpoints, windy coastal locations, or indoors at cafes and visitor centres.

Whisky distillery tours are excellent midge-proof activities — you're indoors, it's interesting, and if you're not riding afterwards, you can sample the product. Museums, castles, and indoor attractions across the Highlands provide alternatives when the midges are at their worst.

Making the Most of Events

Plan your touring calendar around events for maximum value. Ride to Motorcycle Live in Birmingham and extend the trip with a day touring the Shropshire Hills. Attend the TT and spend extra days exploring the Isle of Man's stunning mountain roads. Combine a Welsh rally with a Snowdonia tour.

Events are also excellent places to connect with the riding community. Strike up conversations, join riding groups, and exchange route recommendations. The friendships formed at rallies and shows often lead to shared tours and riding partnerships that last for years.

Planning Around Events

The smartest touring strategy combines events with exploration. Ride to Motorcycle Live in Birmingham and extend the trip with Shropshire Hills touring. Attend a Scottish rally and add three days of Highland riding. Visit the Goodwood Festival of Speed and explore the South Downs and Sussex coast afterward.

Events are also the best places to discover new touring routes. Talk to other riders, collect route recommendations, and note down GPX file sources. The knowledge you gain at a single rally or show can fuel months of future touring. Many events have touring talks, route presentations, and map displays specifically designed to inspire your next ride.

Keep a flexible calendar. Some events are fixed dates (TT, Goodwood), while others shift year to year. Check official websites in January for confirmed dates and build your touring year around the events that matter most to you. faq.q: When is the Scottish midge season?
faq.a: The Highland midge is active from late May to September, peaking from June to August. Dawn and dusk are worst, and they are less active in midday heat and bright sunshine. Still, humid, overcast days bring the worst swarms, especially near water, while wind disperses them, so a breeze of 5mph or more keeps them grounded. Check the Scottish Midge Forecast at smidgeup.com before your tour.

faq.q: Where in Scotland are midges worst?
faq.a: The west Highlands are worst, including Torridon, Kintail and Knoydart, which are the dampest areas with the most midges. They also swarm anywhere near standing water, bogs or damp woodland, and in sheltered valleys and glens with no wind. By contrast, the east coast and mountain summits are generally far less affected, so plan stops accordingly.

faq.q: What repellent actually works against midges?
faq.a: Smidge, a UK-developed repellent containing Saltidin, specifically targets Scottish midges and is highly effective. Avon Skin So Soft Dry Oil Spray is an accidental but genuinely effective repellent famously used by Royal Marines. DEET-based repellents are strong but can damage plastics and synthetics, so use them carefully near motorcycle gear. Citronella is mild and better than nothing.

faq.q: What physical defences help against midges?
faq.a: A midge head net is a fine mesh worn over your head that looks ridiculous but works perfectly and weighs nothing, making it essential for setting up camp. Long sleeves and trousers cover exposed skin because midges cannot bite through clothing. Use a midge-proof tent with mesh fine enough to exclude them, as standard mosquito mesh is too coarse, and choose inner-first designs.

faq.q: How can I keep touring when midges are bad?
faq.a: Riding itself is midge-free, because above walking pace midges cannot keep up, so plan stops at breezy viewpoints, windy coastal spots or indoors at cafes and visitor centres. Camp on high ground or exposed coastal sites where the breeze keeps midges away, avoid stopping near standing water at dawn and dusk, and set up camp quickly before dusk. Distillery tours and museums make good midge-proof alternatives.
